title: Income & Demographics
summary: Who the US consumer actually is: how income is distributed, why spending is 'K-shaped', how credit fuels consumption, and how ethnicity, immigration and household make-up shape demand. Gives you the segmentation instincts interviewers expect in any consumer case.

blocks.title: The median household
blocks.body: US median household income was ~$87K in 2025 (Census), a record high in real terms; after taxes and credits it was ~$76K. The mean is much higher because the top is long-tailed, so always size markets off the median or off tiers, not the average. Spending per household runs ~$78K a year (BLS, 2024), and housing plus transportation take about half of it.

blocks.title: Working income tiers for case segmentation
rows: Budget dominated by rent, food, car; very price- and promotion-sensitive; heavier use of SNAP, dollar stores, BNPL
Mass-market core; trades down selectively, protects a few treats
Drives travel, premium, services; spending tracks stock and home values
~Half of all consumer spending by mid-2025 (Moody's estimate)
blocks.note: Tier cut-offs are rules of thumb for structuring, not official definitions. Pew also adjusts for household size.

blocks.title: The K-shaped consumer
blocks.body: Since 2023 the recovery has split: higher-income households, buoyed by asset gains, keep spending on travel and premium goods, while lower-income households face high rents, food prices and borrowing costs and cut back. Census shows the 90th-percentile household gaining while the 10th percentile was flat in 2025. Moody's estimated the top 10% of earners drove nearly half of spending in Q2 2025, the highest share in its data back to 1989.

blocks.title: Credit and debt: how Americans pay
items: ~82% of adults held a credit card in 2025 (Fed SHED); about 45% of cardholders carried a balance at some point that year.
Credit card balances were ~$1.26T in Q2 2026; total household debt ~$18.8T, of which mortgages ~$13.1T (NY Fed).
Card interest rates are typically 20%+, so revolving balances are expensive; rewards cards subsidize affluent 'transactors'.
~16% of adults used buy now, pay later in 2025, more among lower-income and younger shoppers (Fed SHED).
~63% could cover a $400 surprise expense with cash or equivalent in 2025 (Fed SHED).

blocks.title: Ethnicity, race and immigration as market segments
items: Hispanic Americans: ~70M people, ~21% of the population (July 2025), younger than average (median age ~31); the largest minority group.
Immigrants: ~52M, ~15% of the population (mid-2025, Pew); the first decline since the 1960s came in 2025 as inflows fell.
Top origins: Mexico (~22% of immigrants), then India (~3.2M) and China (2023, Pew); about half from Latin America, ~27% from Asia.
Segments differ in household size, language, media and channel use; treat each as many sub-segments, not one block.
Multicultural shoppers often lead growth in categories like international foods, beauty and remittance/fintech.

blocks.title: Household composition
items: One-person households: ~29% of households (~40M) in 2025, up from 20% in 1975 (Census).
Married couples are now under half of households (~47%); only ~37% of those have kids under 18.
Median age at first marriage: ~31 for men, ~28 for women (2025).
~58% of 18-24 year-olds live with parents (including college dorms); ~16% of 25-34 year-olds do.
~18% of Americans lived in multigenerational households in 2021 (Pew), higher among Asian, Black and Hispanic Americans.

blocks.title: Don't size off the average
blocks.body: Mean income and mean spend are pulled up by the top. For a mass-market product, segment by income tier or use the median. And don't assume a single 'Hispanic' or 'Asian' consumer: origin, generation in the US, language and income vary widely within each group.

blocks.title: Name the K early
blocks.body: In any consumer-demand case, ask 'which income segment is this brand exposed to?' A premium travel brand and a dollar-store chain can read the same macro data in opposite ways. Interviewers reward candidates who split demand by income before projecting a single growth rate.

in_a_case: Declining same-store sales at a mid-tier grocer: check whether core shoppers are lower-income households trading down to Aldi/Walmart rather than blaming store operations.
Market sizing for a premium product: start from ~130M US households (Census: ~129M in 2024), then filter to the top income tiers instead of applying one average spend.
A bank or fintech case: remember most adults hold credit cards and many revolve balances; BNPL and card rewards are segment-specific economics.
Growth strategy for a food brand: Hispanic and Asian American households are fast-growing segments with distinct channel and product preferences.
Product for single-person households: smaller pack sizes, delivery and convenience formats fit the rising share of people living alone.

flashcards.back: ~$87K (Census); ~$76K after taxes and credits. Record high in real terms.
Higher-income households keep spending (asset gains) while lower-income households cut back under high prices and borrowing costs.
